$comment: The releases this project measures itself against, and the facts that identify them.
Read by the `Reference releases are intact` step in release-dmg.yml, which fails the
build if any of these tags disappears or moves to a different commit.
GitHub-side tag protection became available when this repository was made public on
2026-08-17 — rulesets need Pro or a public repository, and it is now the latter. This
check is kept alongside rather than replaced by one: a ruleset can stop a tag being
deleted, but it does not record which commit the tag is supposed to point at, nor the
digest of the artifact that was published from it. Those are the facts a fallback point
is actually made of, and they live here.
Three references. v1.0.5 is the floor, v1.0.9 closes the 1.x line, and v2.5.6 is the
current release, published on 2026-09-12. A release cannot record itself — the commit
it names is the commit that carries it, and no file can contain its own hash — so each
entry here is added by the commit after the release it describes.
v2.5.6 replaced v2.5.5, withdrawn on 2026-09-12 — release, tag and DMG. The same
to v2.1.0 through v2.4.0
on 2026-08-30, so the 2.x line is still represented by its head alone. A reference
cannot be re-cut, so the work that follows one takes a number of its own, and keeping
the list at three means retiring the release it replaces rather than letting both
stand. What that costs is named rather than hidden: a fault introduced this week is no
longer bracketed from below by anything nearer than v1.0.9. The list is kept at three
deliberately; the next reference worth adding is the first 2.x state after this one
that is worth falling back to, and adding it is a decision rather than a consequence of
publishing.
Adding or changing any value below is a deliberate act and shows up in the diff as one.

references.why: First release of the numbering that survives; everything before it was withdrawn.
The second reference: credits the corpus authors, bounds a download that had nothing but the disk to stop it, and is the recent state to fall back to rather than the floor.

The current release and the third reference. It replaced v2.5.5, withdrawn the same day, and the reason the number moved at all is worth recording: the release gate of 2026-09-12 refused to hand out an image built under 2.5.5, because a v2.5.5 with a different digest already stood on the Releases page and the README tells a reader to check that digest. A reference cannot be re-cut, so a bump was the only way out that leaves the instruction true. What it carries over v2.5.5 is what the program knows about the corpus and how safely it publishes. The parser's blind spot was measured: known_limit named four documents where seventeen answered, thirteen of them <AO:-…> names libxml calls a namespace error and exits zero on. Three numbers replace one — 206 refused here, 210 not well-formed XML, 223 objected to by a conforming parser, nesting 206 within 210 within 223 — each with a corpus test holding the names. Two ways to lose a reader's package are closed, each with a test that failed first: the lock file was read without a bound, and a validation failure after publication removed the existing copy before the published tree had been read back. The whole font stack now ships in the repository, Arial written out and no system face left in it, covering 639 of the corpus's 645 code points. The documents themselves are untouched: the byte mirror hashes to 7cfcdce4…35d0 exactly as it did for v2.5.5 and v2.5.4.
